title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (6 of 7)
hook: day three hundred, and Patanjali's three conditions for a practice that holds

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa vairagya: practice and non-attachment, two wings of one bird. Today, the first wing up close.

Three hundred days. However you got here, day after day or in fits and starts, it's a fair place to ask a plain question. Some sittings feel like something. Some feel like nothing at all, like brushing your teeth. So what makes a practice actually hold, not through a week of enthusiasm, but for years? Patanjali answers in a single line, with three conditions, and none of them is feeling good while you do it.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `SOME DAYS, NOTHING AT ALL.` → `WHAT MAKES A PRACTICE HOLD?`

segments.voice: First, thread thirteen defines practice. Abhyasa is the effort to stay there: to remain steady in that stillness. Not the stillness itself, notice. The effort. The returning. So every time you drift and come back, that isn't failure. That's the practice happening. Then thread fourteen: it becomes firmly grounded when it's attended to for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion. A long time: dirgha kala. Not a weekend retreat. Seasons. Years. Without break: nairantarya. The commentators mean steadiness, a thread that keeps running. Some teachers read it kindly: not perfection, but a practice that doesn't wait for ideal conditions. With devotion: satkara, doing something with respect, with care, as if it matters. The same practice done carelessly and done with care are not the same practice. And the result? Dridha bhumi. Firm ground, like soil walked on so many times it becomes a path you can stand on in a storm. Look at what the line leaves out. Patanjali doesn't say you'll feel peaceful every day. He doesn't promise fireworks. He promises ground. Three hundred days is a real start on the first condition.
screen: `PRACTICE IS THE EFFORT TO RETURN.` · `A LONG TIME, WITHOUT BREAK.` · `AND WITH DEVOTION: SATKARA.` · `THE RESULT: FIRM GROUND.` · then, large: `SA TU DĪRGHA-KĀLA-NAIRANTARYA-SATKĀRĀSEVITO DṚḌHA-BHŪMIḤ.`

segments.voice: Treat these minutes with a little extra care: straighten your back as if someone you respect were in the room, and breathe in and out slowly, all the way. When you drift, come back, and count the coming back as the practice, not the drifting as a failure; nothing needs to happen, you're laying ground. If you pray, you can offer these three hundred days to God, the ordinary ones most of all.
Abhyasa, practice, the effort to return. It becomes firm ground over a long time, steadily, with care.
Your line: now. Even an ordinary thing, done with satkara, is practice. Three hundred days, and counting.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often cite 1.14 to explain why daily practice matters more than intensity: a practice kept over a long time, steadily and with respect, becomes firmly grounded.

match.prompt: the three conditions — tap the pairs.

myth: for Patanjali, practice means already being perfectly still
thread thirteen calls practice the effort to stay there: the returning, not the arriving.
thread fourteen names three conditions for a firm practice
a long time, without break, and with devotion.
Patanjali promises you'll feel peaceful every day
he promises firm ground, not daily fireworks.

fork.setup: you drift off during practice for the tenth time today. what is that moment, for Patanjali?
options: a sign to stop for the day.
the practice: the effort of coming back.
fork.reveal: thread thirteen defines practice as the effort to stay steady, which means the returning is the practice itself.

original.note: Sanskrit: practice, repeated effort; from abhi + as, to apply oneself to something again and again.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strong practice means intense sessions.
what it means: a long time, without break, with care; the result is firm ground.
what a scholar hears: satkara, respect or reverent attention, is the third condition in 1.14; dridha-bhumi, 'firm ground', is the image of a practice that can no longer be easily shaken.
guess: the effort of coming back, again and again
a perfect sitting with no stray thoughts

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 1.13 (tatra sthitau yatno 'bhyasah: practice is the effort to be steady there)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook told the listener they had opened the app 'three hundred times' and how those days 'probably felt', and claimed Patanjali was 'clearly writing for people who struggle'; rewritten. 'Teachers who know real lives' (implied others don't) softened; stock 'quiet good news' cut; the 'going back toward' etymology in the original note replaced with the standard abhi + as gloss.
The etymology in the original note ('going back toward', abhi + as) is a popular gloss; the root is usually given as abhi + as, 'to apply oneself repeatedly'. Confirm or simplify.
Nairantarya read kindly as steadiness rather than perfection is a pastoral reading, presented as 'teachers who know real lives read it kindly'. Confirm.
The sutra is quoted in IAST on screen (the large line) and in sources.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
